title: Processes and systems for recapturing carbon from biomass pyrolysis liquids
text: Processes and systems for recapturing carbon from biomass pyrolysis liquids This disclosure provides a method of making a high-fixed-carbon material comprising pyrolyzing biomass to generate intermediate solids and a pyrolysis vapor; condensing the pyrolysis vapor to generate pyrolysis liquid; blending the pyrolysis liquid with the intermediate solids, to generate a mixture; and further pyrolyzing the mixture to generate a high-fixed-carbon material. A process can comprise: pyrolyzing a biomass-comprising feedstock in a first pyrolysis reactor to generate a first biogenic reagent and a first pyrolysis vapor; introducing the first pyrolysis vapor to a condensing system to generate a condenser liquid; contacting the first biogenic reagent with the condenser liquid, thereby generating an intermediate material; further pyrolyzing the intermediate material in a second pyrolysis reactor to generate a second biogenic reagent and a second pyrolysis vapor; and recovering the second biogenic reagent as a high-yield biocarbon composition. The process can further comprise pelletizing the intermediate material. Many process and system configurations are disclosed. This disclosure provides a method of making a high-fixed-carbon material comprising pyrolyzing biomass to generate intermediate solids and a pyrolysis vapor; condensing the pyrolysis vapor to generate pyrolysis liquid; blending the pyrolysis liquid with the intermediate solids, to generate a mixture; and further pyrolyzing the mixture to generate a high-fixed-carbon material. A process can comprise: pyrolyzing a biomass-comprising feedstock in a first pyrolysis reactor to generate a first biogenic reagent and a first pyrolysis vapor; introducing the first pyrolysis vapor to a condensing system to generate a condenser liquid; contacting the first biogenic reagent with the condenser liquid, thereby generating an intermediate material; further pyrolyzing the intermediate material in a second pyrolysis reactor to generate a second biogenic reagent and a second pyrolysis vapor; and recovering the second biogenic reagent as a high-yield biocarbon composition. The process can further comprise pelletizing the intermediate material. Many process and system configurations are disclosed. The application claims the priority benefit of U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. 63/228,536, filed on Aug. 2, 2021, which is incorporated by reference herein in its entirety. The present technology generally relates to pyrolysis processes utilizing recapture of carbon from pyrolysis oil, for making high-yield biocarbon compositions. Carbon is a platform element in a wide variety of industries and has a vast number of chemical, material, and fuel uses. Carbon is a good fuel to produce energy, including electricity. Carbon also has tremendous chemical value for various commodities and advanced materials, including metals, metal alloys, composites, carbon fibers, electrodes, and catalyst supports. For metal making, carbon is useful as a reactant, for reducing metal oxides to metals during processing; as a fuel, to provide heat for processing; and as a component of a metal alloy. Carbon can be produced, in principle, from virtually any carbonaceous material. Carbonaceous materials commonly include fossil resources such as natural gas, petroleum, coal, and lignite; and renewable resources such as lignocellulosic biomass and various carbon-rich waste materials. It is preferable to utilize renewable biomass to produce carbon-based reagents because of the rising economic, environmental, and social costs associated with fossil resources. Biomass is a term used to describe any biologically produced matter, or biogenic matter. The chemical energy contained in biomass is derived from solar energy using the natural process of photosynthesis. Photosynthesis is the process by which plants take in carbon dioxide and water from their surroundings and, using energy from sunlight, convert them into sugars, starches, cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Of all the renewable energy sources, biomass is unique in that it is, effectively, stored solar energy. Furthermore, biomass is the only renewable source of carbon. There exist a variety of conversion technologies to turn biomass feedstocks into high-carbon materials. Pyrolysis is a process for thermal conversion of solid materials in the complete absence of oxidizing agent (air or oxygen), or with such limited supply that oxidation does not occur to any appreciable extent. Depending on process conditions and additives, biomass pyrolysis can be adjusted to produce widely varying amounts of gas, liquid, and solid. Lower process temperatures and longer vapor residence times favor the production of solids. High temperatures and longer residence times increase the biomass conversion to syngas, while moderate temperatures and short vapor residence times are generally optimum for producing liquids. Historically, slow pyrolysis of wood has been performed in large piles, in a simple batch process, with no emissions control. Traditional charcoal-making technologies are energy-inefficient as well as highly polluting. There is a desire for improved or optimized processes for producing biocarbon compositions, especially with respect to carbon yield and biocarbon properties. In some embodiments, the process further comprises pelletizing the first biogenic reagent. In these or other embodiments, the process can further comprise pelletizing the intermediate material. In certain embodiments, pelletizing the intermediate material is integrated with the step of contacting the first biogenic reagent with the condenser liquid. In other embodiments, pelletizing the intermediate material occurs after contacting the first biogenic reagent with the condenser liquid. Pelletizing the intermediate material, when performed, can include introducing a binder to the intermediate material. The carbon recapture unit can be a mixing unit contacting the first biogenic reagent with the condenser liquid. Alternatively, or additionally, a carbon recapture unit can be distinct from a mixing unit. A carbon recapture unit can be fed a carbon source different than the condenser liquid, such as an external carbon source or a waste carbon-containing stream from the process. In certain embodiments, the plurality of stages does not include the final stage of the multiple condenser stages, especially when the final stage is configured or operated such that the final condenser product contains a high concentration of water. In some embodiments, the intermediate material comprises the condenser liquid adsorbed onto a surface of the first biogenic reagent. Alternatively, or additionally, the intermediate material can comprise the condenser liquid absorbed into a bulk phase of the first biogenic reagent. In some embodiments, the thermal-treatment unit is a second pyrolysis reactor operated at a temperature of at least about 250Â° C., wherein the second pyrolysis reactor is configured for pyrolyzing the intermediate material. In other embodiments, the thermal-treatment unit is operated at a relatively low temperature selected from about 80Â° C. to about 250Â° C., for example. title: Methods and systems for pyrolysis and carbon deposition
text: Methods and systems for pyrolysis and carbon deposition The present invention provides a method of sequentially pyrolysing and depositing carbon to produce a composite carbonaceous product, the method comprising a pyrolysis process step comprising pyrolysing a pyrolysable organic feed in a first reaction zone in the presence of a non-oxidizing gas at a pyrolysis temperature to produce hot char and a pyrolysis gas, wherein the pyrolysis gas and the non-oxidizing gas combine to form a gas mixture, discharging the gas mixture from the first reaction zone to a combustion zone and combusting at least a portion of the pyrolysis gas in the combustion zone, wherein heat generated by combustion of the pyrolysis gas is transferred from the combustion zone to the first reaction zone to provide at least a portion of the hot char, and a decomposition process step comprising directly contacting a hydrocarbon-rich organic gas with the hot char after the hot char is produced in the pyrolysis process step, wherein the hydrocarbon-rich organic gas is catalytically decomposed on the hot char at a decomposition temperature above the pyrolysis temperature to produce a gaseous decomposition product comprising hydrogen and a composite carbonaceous material comprising char having carbonaceous deposits thereon. The present invention provides a method of sequentially pyrolysing and depositing carbon to produce a composite carbonaceous product, the method comprising a pyrolysis process step comprising pyrolysing a pyrolysable organic feed in a first reaction zone in the presence of a non-oxidizing gas at a pyrolysis temperature to produce hot char and a pyrolysis gas, wherein the pyrolysis gas and the non-oxidizing gas combine to form a gas mixture, discharging the gas mixture from the first reaction zone to a combustion zone and combusting at least a portion of the pyrolysis gas in the combustion zone, wherein heat generated by combustion of the pyrolysis gas is transferred from the combustion zone to the first reaction zone to provide at least a portion of the hot char, and a decomposition process step comprising directly contacting a hydrocarbon-rich organic gas with the hot char after the hot char is produced in the pyrolysis process step, wherein the hydrocarbon-rich organic gas is catalytically decomposed on the hot char at a decomposition temperature above the pyrolysis temperature to produce a gaseous decomposition product comprising hydrogen and a composite carbonaceous material comprising char having carbonaceous deposits thereon. The present invention relates to a method and system for sequential pyrolysis and carbon deposition to produce a composite carbonaceous product. The method includes pyrolyzing an organic feed to produce hot char and pyrolysis gases, combusting the pyrolysis gases and transferring heat from the combustion to provide at least a portion of the heat of heat, and catalytically decomposing the hydrocarbon-rich organic gases directly on the hot char at a temperature above the pyrolysis temperature after the hot char is produced. Thereby producing a composite carbonaceous material comprising char having carbon deposits thereon. Carbon emissions are of increasing interest in many industrial processes, including processes that seek to repair or monetize biomass or carbonaceous waste materials. Gasification and incineration have been proposed as thermal methods for treating such feedstocks, but almost all of the carbon is ultimately emitted in the form of carbon dioxide. Another method by which a portion of the feedstock carbon may advantageously be retained in a stable solid product is pyrolysis. Pyrolysis is a pyrolysis process for converting a pyrolysable organic feed (i.e., any feed containing at least a portion of an organic carbon-based material) under non-oxidizing conditions, particularly where the oxygen content is low enough that an endothermic cracking reaction predominates over an exothermic oxidation reaction. Industrial pyrolysis is typically run at medium to high temperatures (350-900 â) to produce products for energy, fuel or chemical applications. Pyrolysis produces three product streams, a solid carbonaceous product (char), a condensable pyrolysis oil portion, and a non-condensable gas portion. Pyrolysis is considered particularly useful for treating waste or biomass streams (including biosolids that are products of wastewater treatment plants) that may be contaminated. Pyrolysis advantageously sterilizes potentially harmful microorganisms in the feedstock and permanently sequesters a portion of the carbon in the (bio) char product. However, other carbonaceous streams (including biogas) that are typically co-produced with solid feedstock are typically combusted. The pyrolysis product may be converted into useful derivatives, or may be used in its original form for many applications. For example, the char may be used for soil improvement, soil remediation, water purification, composite materials, or as a fuel. However, given the cost of repairing or utilizing the running process of low value waste feedstock, there is a need to increase the value of the product train, particularly the solid pyrolysis product. During pyrolysis where char is the primary target product, the oil portion and/or the gas portion may be burned to provide the energy required to drive the endothermic pyrolysis reaction. The excess energy may be used to generate electricity or utility steam. A further problem in such pyrolysis systems is that the heat transfer between combustion and pyrolysis may be unsatisfactory, resulting in poor heat distribution, and therefore low pyrolysis rates and/or poor or inconsistent quality char products. Furthermore, there remains a need to improve the overall energy balance of pyrolysis systems. Chemical Vapor Deposition (CVD) is another method of carbon sequestration, in this case by carbon deposition in the form of carbon nanomaterials. The gaseous hydrocarbon vapor is passed over a catalyst to produce carbon nanomaterial and hydrogen-enriched decomposition gas products. Synthetic catalysts for this process have been reported, including catalytic metals such as Ni, fe and Co. However, such catalysts are easily deactivated and must be regenerated because they are expensive. They also leave metallic impurities in the carbon nanomaterial. Accordingly, lower cost carbon-based catalysts such as activated carbon, graphite, and carbon black have been proposed as alternatives to metal catalysts. However, the conversion obtained using carbon-based catalysts is relatively low compared to synthetic catalysts. In addition, carbon-based catalysts are either purchased or produced from specialized raw materials in a separate process prior to use in CVD. Thus, the cost of producing carbon-based catalysts with adequate performance remains a limiting factor in the implementation of large-scale CVD processes. Pyrolysis processes have been reported in which increased overall carbon recovery is obtained by readsorption and dehydrogenation of pyrolysis vapors on the char pyrolysis product, either simultaneously with the pyrolysis reaction occurring in the pyrolysis reaction zone or separately in downstream process units. However, at the typical pyrolysis temperatures at which these dehydrogenation reactions occur, amorphous coke deposits that block the pores form on the char, rather than a valorized carbon material such as a carbon nanomaterial. Accordingly, there is a continuing need for new methods and systems of pyrolysis and carbon deposition that address, at least in part, one or more of the above-described disadvantages or provide a useful alternative. The reference herein to a patent document or other matter which is given as prior art is not to be taken as an admission that the document or matter was known or that the information it contains was part of the common general knowledge as at the priority date of any of the claims. According to a first aspect, the present invention provides a method of sequential pyrolysis and carbon deposition to produce a composite carbonaceous product, the method comprising a pyrolysis process step comprising pyrolyzing a pyrolyzable organic feed in a first reaction zone at a pyrolysis temperature in the presence of a non-oxidizing gas to produce hot char and a pyrolysis gas, wherein the pyrolysis gas and the non-oxidizing gas combine to form a gas mixture, discharging the gas mixture from the first reaction zone to a combustion zone, and combusting at least a portion of the pyrolysis gas in the combustion zone, wherein heat generated by combustion of the pyrolysis gas is transferred from the combustion zone to the first reaction zone to provide at least a portion of the hot fever, and a decomposition process step comprising directly contacting a hydrocarbon-rich organic gas with the hot char after the hot char is produced in the pyrolysis process step, wherein the hydrocarbon-rich organic gas is catalytically decomposed on the hot char at a decomposition temperature above the pyrolysis temperature to produce a gaseous decomposition product comprising hydrogen and a composite carbonaceous material comprising carbonaceous deposits thereon. Advantageously, the integrated mode of sequential pyrolysis and carbon deposition process steps can provide a high degree of sequestration of overall carbon from both carbonaceous feeds in a stable and potentially useful composite carbonaceous product. The immediate use of the formed hot char pyrolysis product as a carbon deposition catalyst may provide improved catalytic performance compared to a similar preformed material on the surface, as the cooling-induced degradation mechanism is minimized. Furthermore, since the intermediate carbon product, which already contains process heat, is used as a catalytic substrate for high temperature carbon deposition, a high degree of thermal efficiency can be obtained. The temperature rise between the pyrolysis and decomposition process steps helps to form high quality crystalline carbon materials, including carbon nanomaterials. The combustion of the pyrolysis gas and optionally also the decomposition gas is used to provide the heat required for the endothermic reaction. In some embodiments, the method further comprises separating a gas composition comprising gaseous decomposition products and any residual hydrocarbon-rich organic gas from the composite carbonaceous material and combusting at least a portion of the combustible components therein, wherein heat generated by combustion of the combustible components is transferred to provide at least a portion of the decomposition heat. In some embodiments, the pyrolyzable organic feed comprises biomass, such as biosolids. In some embodiments, the thermal char is continuously maintained at a temperature above 300 â, or above 400 â, or above 600 â, or above 700 â, between the generation of the thermal char in the pyrolysis process step and the catalytic decomposition of the hydrocarbon-rich organic gas on the thermal char in the decomposition process step. In some embodiments, the pyrolysis in the pyrolysis process step and the catalytic decomposition in the decomposition process step are performed sequentially in the first reaction zone. Catalytic decomposition can be initiated by introducing a hydrocarbon-rich organic gas into the first reaction zone. When introducing a hydrocarbon rich organic gas stream, the flow of non-oxidizing gas into the first reaction zone may be reduced or stopped. The solids in the first reaction zone may be continuously fluidized in a fluidized stream comprising non-oxidizing gas and/or hydrocarbon rich organic gas during pyrolysis and catalytic decomposition. In some embodiments, the first reaction zone is separated from the combustion zone by a heat transfer barrier, wherein heat transferred from the combustion zone to the first reaction zone to provide at least a portion of the heat of heat is transferred through the heat transfer barrier. The heat transfer barrier may comprise a plurality of holes through which the gas mixture flows from the first reaction zone into the combustion zone. In some such embodiments, catalytic decomposition in the decomposition process step is performed in a first reaction zone and the gaseous composition comprising gaseous decomposition products and any residual hydrocarbon-rich organic gas is discharged to a combustion zone to combust combustible components in the combustion zone, wherein heat generated by combustion of the combustible components is transferred through a heat transfer barrier to provide at least a portion of the decomposition heat. In some embodiments, the hydrocarbon-rich organic gas is substantially free of pyrolysis gases or components thereof produced during the pyrolysis process step. Thus, all or substantially all (e.g., greater than 90%) of the hydrocarbon-rich organic gas may be provided from a source external to the pyrolysis process step that generates the hot char. In some embodiments, the hydrocarbon-rich organic gas is selected from biogas and plastic pyrolysis gas. In some embodiments, the method further comprises pyrolyzing the polymer to produce hot pyrolysis vapors, wherein the hot pyrolysis vapors form at least a portion of the hydrocarbon-rich organic gas, separating a gas composition comprising gaseous decomposition products and any residual hydrocarbon-rich organic gas from the composite carbonaceous material, and cooling the gas composition to condense a pyrolysis oil portion. In some embodiments, the method further comprises withdrawing a portion of the gas mixture from the first reaction zone, wherein the pyrolysis gas in the first reaction zone forms at least a portion of the hydrocarbon-rich organic gas. In some embodiments, the decomposition temperature is at least 700 â, or at least 750 â, or at least 800 â, such as at least 850 â. In some embodiments, the decomposition temperature is no more than 200 â higher than the pyrolysis temperature, or no more than 100 â higher. In some embodiments, the method further comprises introducing an activating additive into the first reaction zone prior to or during pyrolysis, wherein the activating additive results in an increase in the surface area of the hot char relative to the hot char produced in the absence of the additive. The activating additive may be selected from NaOH and KOH. In some embodiments, the composite carbonaceous material comprises at least 5wt% carbon deposit, or at least 10 wt% carbon deposit, or at least 20 wt% carbon deposit. In some embodiments, the carbon deposit is crystalline. In some embodiments, the carbon deposit comprises a carbon nanomaterial, for example selected from the group consisting of carbon nanotubes, carbon nanofibers, and carbon nanospheres. In some embodiments, at least 30% or at least 40% of the total carbon in the pyrolyzable organic feed and hydrocarbon rich organic gas is sequestered in the composite carbonaceous material. In some embodiments, the method includes separating and recovering at least a portion of the hydrogen. Such a method may include separating a gas composition comprising gaseous decomposition products and any residual hydrocarbon-rich organic gas from the composite carbonaceous material, and separating hydrogen from the gas composition. In some embodiments, the method further comprises generating electrical energy and/or steam from heat generated from combustion of combustible components in the pyrolysis gas and/or gas composition comprising gaseous decomposition products and any residual hydrocarbon-rich organic gas. According to a second aspect, the present invention provides a system for sequential pyrolysis and carbon deposition to produce a composite carbonaceous product, the system comprising (i) a first The system may include one or more heat exchange conduits configured to convey combustion product gas from the combustion zone through the first reaction zone to heat the fluidized solids in use. Embodiments of the present invention will now be described, by way of example only, with reference to the accompanying drawings, in which: Fig. 1 schematically depicts a system for sequential pyrolysis and carbon deposition in the same reaction zone according to an embodiment of the present invention. The present invention relates to a method of sequentially pyrolysing and depositing carbon to produce a composite carbonaceous product. The method includes a pyrolysis process step that includes pyrolyzing a pyrolysable organic feed in a first reaction zone in the presence of a non-oxidizing gas to produce hot char and pyrolysis gas. The pyrolysis gas and the non-oxidizing gas combine to form a gas mixture, some or all of which is discharged from the first reaction zone to the combustion zone. At least a portion of the pyrolysis gases are combusted in the combustion zone, and heat generated by the combustion is transferred from the combustion zone to the first reaction zone to provide at least a portion of the heat removal. The method further includes a decomposition process step comprising directly contacting a hydrocarbon-rich organic gas with the hot char after the hot char is produced in the pyrolysis process step. Catalytically decomposing the hydrocarbon-rich organic gas on the hot char at a decomposition temperature above the pyrolysis temperature, thereby producing a gaseous decomposition product comprising hydrogen and a composite carbonaceous material comprising char having carbon deposits thereon. Depicted in fig. 1 is a system 100 according to an embodiment of the present invention. The system 100 includes a reaction vessel having a first reaction zone 120, a feed inlet 122 for introducing an organic pyrolyzable feed 124, a gas inlet 126, a solid product outlet 128, and one or more gas outlets 130. The gas inlet 126 is supplied by a gas manifold comprising valves 132 and 134 which control the flow of non-oxidizing gas 136 and hydrocarbon rich organic gas 138, respectively. Alternatively, valves 132 and 134 may control the addition of gases 136 and 138 to the first reaction zone through separate gas inlets. In some embodiments, the reaction zone 120 is configured to fluidize solids in a gas stream introduced through the inlet 126. The system 100 further includes a combustion zone 140, which may be a separate reaction zone within the same reaction vessel as the first reaction zone 120 or in a different reaction vessel. The combustion zone 140 is provided with one or more feed gas inlets 142 for feeding the gas mixture 144 exiting the first reaction zone 120, an oxidizing gas inlet 146 for introducing an oxygen-containing gas 148, and a combustion gas outlet 150 for discharging a combustion product gas 152. The combustion zone 140 and the first reaction zone 120 are thermally integrated such that heat 154 generated by the exothermic combustion reaction in the combustion zone 140 can be transferred to the first reaction zone 120 to drive the endothermic reaction therein. This can be accomplished in a variety of ways, including using a heat exchanger to preheat the feed gas entering the first reaction zone 120 or by using a heat transfer barrier between the reaction zone 120 and the combustion zone 140, as will be described in more detail below. In use, a non-oxidizing gas 136, such as nitrogen, is fed to the first reaction zone 120 by opening the valve 132 while maintaining the valve 134 closed. A pyrolyzable organic feed 124, such as biosolids in particulate form, is fed to the first reaction zone 124 for pyrolysis in the presence of a non-oxidizing gas. Optionally, the solid feed is fluidized in a non-oxidizing gas stream. Pyrolysis is performed at conventional pyrolysis temperatures, such as 350 â to 900 â (depending on the feed) to produce char and pyrolysis gases. The low oxygen content in the non-oxidizing gas 136 advantageously facilitates selectivity to the desired pyrolytic cracking reaction as opposed to the undesired oxidation reaction. The pyrolysis reaction is conducted in this manner for a solids residence time sufficient to convert the feed 124 to char, typically 30 minutes to 6 hours. During this time, the pyrolysis gas combines with the non-oxidizing gas 136 to form a gas mixture 144 that is discharged from the first reaction zone 120 through the gas outlet 130. The gas mixture 144 is fed to the combustion zone 140 through a feed gas inlet 142 where it is contacted with an oxygen-containing gas 148 (e.g., air), the oxygen-containing gas 148 being introduced through an oxidizing gas inlet 146. At least some of the combustible pyrolysis gas components in the gas mixture are combusted in the combustion zone 140 to form combustion product gases 152 and heat. Combustion product gas 152 exits combustion zone 140 through combustion gas outlet 150. Heat 154 generated in the combustion is transferred from the combustion zone 140 to the first reaction zone 120 to provide all or part of the heat removal to maintain the desired pyrolysis reaction temperature. In some embodiments, combustion in the combustion zone 140 is controlled such that all of the pyrolysis gases are substantially completely combusted. Oxygen-containing gas 148 is thus added in excess such that combustion product gas 152 contains a significant amount of residual oxygen. The excess heat of combustion generated in the combustion zone 140 can optionally be used to generate electricity or steam by conventional means. The combustion product gas 152 may then be sent directly to post-combustion clean-up and emissions. In other embodiments, the addition of the oxygen-containing gas 148 to the combustion zone 140 is limited such that a significant amount of residual unburned (or partially burned) components are present in the combustion product gas 152. For example, the addition of gas 148, and thus the degree of oxidation in combustion zone 140, may be a controllable variable for maintaining the pyrolysis temperature in reaction zone 120 within a desired range. In this case, the partially combusted product gas 152 may be sent to another combustor (not shown) where the remaining combustible products therein are combusted in the presence of excess oxygen to extinction, optionally using heat to generate electricity or steam. After a selected period of time to convert the organic feed 124 to char, valve 134 is opened to introduce a stream of hydrocarbon rich organic gas 138 (e.g., biogas) into the first reaction zone. Optionally, the flow of non-oxidizing gas 136 is simultaneously reduced or completely stopped. In fluidized bed embodiments, the solids in the first reaction zone can thus be continuously fluidized in a fluidized stream of gas, ensuring continuous good mixing and heat transfer. The hot char in the reactor preferably does not substantially cool during the change in gas feed composition, in effect operating the system 100, such as by adding transfer heat 154 or by preheating the hydrocarbon rich organic gas 138, to raise the temperature in the reaction zone 120 to the desired decomposition temperature before or after the introduction of the hydrocarbon rich organic gas 138. At least a portion of the hydrocarbons in the hydrocarbon rich organic gas 138 are thus catalytically decomposed on the hot char in the first reaction zone 120 at a decomposition temperature above the pyrolysis temperature (or temperature range) for producing char, thereby forming carbon nanomaterial deposits on the char and producing hydrogen. The elevated decomposition temperature may help to form a higher quality, more carbonaceous and crystalline material and produce higher yields of hydrogen than pyrolysis. Without wishing to be bound by any theory, it is also believed that the carbon deposition reaction is aided by the further pyrolytic release of volatile components from the char itself that occurs at the elevated temperature. The decomposition process step may be carried out at temperatures in excess of 600 â, such as 700 â to 1000 â. The decomposition temperature can affect the rate of decomposition and the morphology of the carbon deposit. The inventors have found that at 700 â methane decomposes on certain biochars to produce carbon nanofiber deposits, and at 900 â methane or other organic gases decompose on biochars to produce carbon nanospheres or carbon nanotube deposits. Higher decomposition temperatures, such as above 800 â, or 900 â and higher, may be particularly desirable. The low oxygen content already present in the first reaction zone 120 and in the feed of hydrocarbon rich organic gas 138 advantageously facilitates selectivity to the desired decomposition reaction as opposed to the undesired oxidation reaction. The decomposition reaction is carried out in this way for a period of time sufficient to form carbon deposits on the char. This period of time may be less than 5 hours, or less than 1 hour, such as less than 30 minutes, due to the rapid rate of deactivation. During this time, hydrogen and any other gaseous products combine with residual gas 138 to form gas mixture 144a, which is discharged from first reaction zone 120 through gas outlet 130. The gas mixture 144a is fed to the combustion zone 140 through a feed gas inlet 142 where it is contacted with an oxygen-containing gas 148 (e.g., air), the oxygen-containing gas 148 being introduced through an oxidizing gas inlet 146. At least some of the combustible components (including hydrogen) in the gas mixture are combusted in the combustion zone 140 to form combustion product gas 152a and heat. Combustion product gas 152a exits combustion zone 140 through combustion gas outlet 150. Heat 154a generated in the combustion is transferred from the combustion zone 140 to the first reaction zone 120 to provide all or part of the decomposition heat to maintain the desired decomposition reaction temperature. Combustion may be controlled during the decomposition phase, as during the pyrolysis phase, to fully or partially combust all of the combustible components in the gas mixture 144 a. If combustion is limited such that a significant amount of residual hydrogen remains in the combustion product gas 152a, this hydrogen may be combusted in a further downstream combustion unit or recovered as a hydrogen source. Once the decomposition process steps are completed, valve 134 may be closed and valve 132 opened. The composite carbonaceous product 146 is unloaded from the first reaction zone, comprising char having carbon deposits thereon. A further amount of organic feed 124 is then added to initiate a new pyrolysis process step. The system 100 is thus operated by successive cycles of pyrolysis and carbon deposition. Advantageously, the integrated mode of sequential pyrolysis and carbon deposition that can be achieved in the system 100 provides a high degree of sequestration of total carbon from the pyrolyzable organic feed and hydrocarbon rich organic gas in a stable composite carbonaceous product. It is estimated that 30% to 50% of the total carbon can be sequestered. The composite has wide potential applications in soil improvement, soil remediation, water purification, environmental remediation, and advanced materials (e.g., for battery storage and catalysts). It is also believed that successive pyrolysis-carbon deposition involving the immediate use of a hot char pyrolysis product as a carbon deposition catalyst will provide higher hydrocarbon-rich gas conversion and/or higher quality carbon nanomaterial deposits in the decomposition reaction than would be possible using a similar preformed material on the surface. Cooling of the pyrolytic carbon results in a permanent decrease in pore size due to uneven condensation, solidification, nucleation and polymerization reactions. In addition, the gaseous pyrolysis vapors may condense and react on the carbon surface to form an amorphous carbonaceous or tar layer and plug pores. This undesirable change is irreversible upon reheating. A high degree of thermal efficiency is achieved in the system 100 because i) the intermediate char product is immediately used as a matrix for high temperature carbon deposition in subsequent reactions without extensive cooling, and ii) the combustion of pyrolysis gases and decomposition gases serves to maintain a continuous high temperature and drive the endothermic reaction in the reaction zone. Thus, the energy requirements of the system 100 are low and in fact an advantageous positive energy balance can be obtained, allowing the generation of electricity and/or steam. The system 100 has the further advantage of a simple process, which is highly desirable in many environments where pyrolysis, particularly pyrolysis of biomass such as biosolids, is performed. Pyrolysis and catalytic decomposition reactions are carried out sequentially using a single reaction zone in a gas feed switching mode without transferring solids from one reaction zone to another. The conversion is readily controlled by simply introducing a hydrocarbon-rich organic gas feed into the reaction zone, while optionally correspondingly reducing the initial feed of non-oxidizing gas. Depicted in fig. 2 is a pyrolysis system 200 according to another embodiment of the present invention. Similarly numbered objects of system 200 are as described herein with respect to system 100 depicted in fig. 1. However, in system 200, first reaction zone 220 is not necessarily configured to feed hydrocarbon-rich organic gas. Instead, the system 200 includes a second reaction zone 260, which may be a separate reaction zone within the same reaction vessel as the first reaction zone 220 or in a different reaction vessel. The second reaction zone 260 is provided with a char inlet 262, an organic gas inlet 264, a solids outlet 266, and one or more decomposition gas outlets 268. The system 200 is configured such that the hot char 246 may be discharged from the first reaction zone 220 into the second reaction zone 260. For example, the system 200 may include a rotary kiln or an augur type reactor that transfers the pyrolysable organic feed through the first reaction zone 220 where it is subjected to pyrolysis conditions in the presence of a non-oxidizing gas 236, for a suitable residence time, and into the second reaction zone 260. The system 200 also includes a combustion zone 240, which may be a separate reaction zone within the same reaction vessel as the first reaction zone 220 or in a different reaction vessel. As described for system 100, combustion zone 240 and first reaction zone 220 are thermally integrated such that heat 254 generated by the exothermic combustion reaction in combustion zone 240 can be transferred to first reaction zone 120 to drive the endothermic pyrolysis reaction therein. The system 200 may optionally include an additional combustion zone 280 configured to receive and combust the gas mixture exiting the second reaction zone 260. The combustion zone 280 (if present) can optionally be thermally integrated with the second reaction zone 260 such that heat 274 generated by the exothermic combustion reaction in the combustion zone 280 can be transferred to the second reaction zone 260 to drive the endothermic decomposition reaction therein. In use, the pyrolysable organic feed 224 is fed to the first reaction zone 220 and pyrolysed in the presence of the non-oxidising gas 236 to form hot char and pyrolysis gas. The system 200 may be operated in a continuous mode, so the feed 224 may be a continuous feed. The pyrolysis gases combine with the non-oxidizing gases 236 to form a gas mixture 244 that is discharged from the first reaction zone 220 into the combustion zone 240. At least a portion of the pyrolysis gases are then combusted in the combustion zone 240, as described for the system 100, with heat being used to drive the endothermic pyrolysis reaction in the first reaction zone 220. After a suitable residence time for conversion of the organic feed 224, the hot char is discharged into the second reaction zone 260 through the solid product outlet 228 and char inlet 262. The hot char preferably does not substantially cool during the transfer process, and the transfer may optionally be performed continuously. A hydrocarbon rich organic gas 238, such as biogas or plastic pyrolysis gas, is fed to the second reaction zone 260 where at least a portion of the hydrocarbons in the gas are catalytically decomposed on the hot char at a decomposition temperature above the pyrolysis temperature (or temperature range) in the first reaction zone 220 where char is produced. Thus forming carbon nanomaterial deposits on the char and generating hydrogen gas. The decomposition may be carried out at temperatures exceeding 600 â, preferably exceeding 650 â, such as 700 â to 1000 â. The hydrogen and any other gaseous products combine with the residual gas 238 to form a gaseous mixture 272 that is discharged from the second reaction zone 260 through the decomposition gas outlet 268. After a suitable residence time in the second reaction zone 260, a composite carbonaceous product 270 is unloaded from the second reaction zone, which comprises char having carbon deposits thereon. Although the system 200 may be operated continuously, it is still a process for sequential pyrolysis and carbon deposition because the char is first formed during the pyrolysis process step and then carbon deposits are deposited thereon during the decomposition process step. The gas mixture 272 may optionally be sent to a burner 280 to combust combustible components therein, and the heat of combustion 274 may optionally be transferred to the second reaction zone 260 to drive an endothermic decomposition reaction therein. Alternatively, the second reaction zone 260 may be heated in an alternative manner and hydrogen may be recovered from the gas mixture 168. As with system 100, system 200 also provides an integrated mode of sequential pyrolysis and carbon deposition that sequesters large amounts of carbon from both carbonaceous feeds in a stable carbonaceous composite. Similarly, the system 200 also provides thermal efficiency due to the substantial lack of cooling by transfer of the hot char intermediate and thermal integration between combustion and at least pyrolysis reactions. In addition, system 200 provides the potential advantage of being continuously operable. Continuous operation is advantageous in terms of process stability, especially in larger scale units. In one variation of process 200, pyrolysis gas stream 244a, which comprises a portion of the pyrolysis gas products mixed with non-oxidizing gas 236, is withdrawn from first reaction zone 220 and conveyed outwardly to form at least a portion of hydrocarbon rich organic gas 238, which is fed to second reaction zone 260. There, at least a portion of the hydrocarbons in the pyrolysis gas are catalytically decomposed on the hot char at a decomposition temperature above the pyrolysis temperature in the first reaction zone 220, thereby forming carbon nanomaterial deposits on the char and producing hydrogen. The elevated decomposition temperature favors the desired decomposition reaction to form high quality crystalline carbon deposits, preferably comprising carbon nanomaterials. In contrast, the pyrolysis temperature may be too low to allow significant decomposition of the pyrolysis gases during the pyrolysis process steps. Also in this embodiment, a portion of the pyrolysis gas is sent to and combusted in the combustion zone 240 via the gas mixture 244 to drive the endothermic pyrolysis reaction. Further details of each processing unit in the system of the invention and steps of the method of the invention will now be described.

title: Bio-reduction of metal ores integrated with biomass pyrolysis
text: Bio-reduction of metal ores integrated with biomass pyrolysis Some variations provide a composition for reducing a metal ore, the composition comprising a carbon-metal ore particulate, wherein the carbon-metal ore particulate comprises at least about 0.1 wt % to at most about 50 wt % fixed carbon on a moisture-free and ash-free basis, and wherein the carbon is at least 50% renewable carbon as determined from a measurement of the 14 C/ 12 C isotopic ratio. Some variations provide a process for reducing a metal ore, comprising: providing a biomass feedstock; pyrolyzing the feedstock to generate a biogenic reagent comprising carbon and a pyrolysis off-gas comprising hydrogen or carbon monoxide; obtaining a metal ore comprising a metal oxide; combining the carbon with the metal ore, to generate a carbon-metal ore particulate; optionally pelletizing the carbon-metal ore particulate; and utilizing the pyrolysis off-gas to chemically reduce the metal oxide to elemental metal, such as iron. Some variations provide a composition for reducing a metal ore, the composition comprising a carbon-metal ore particulate, wherein the carbon-metal ore particulate comprises at least about 0.1 wt % to at most about 50 wt % fixed carbon on a moisture-free and ash-free basis, and wherein the carbon is at least 50% renewable carbon as determined from a measurement of the 14 C/ 12 C isotopic ratio. Some variations provide a process for reducing a metal ore, comprising: providing a biomass feedstock; pyrolyzing the feedstock to generate a biogenic reagent comprising carbon and a pyrolysis off-gas comprising hydrogen or carbon monoxide; obtaining a metal ore comprising a metal oxide; combining the carbon with the metal ore, to generate a carbon-metal ore particulate; optionally pelletizing the carbon-metal ore particulate; and utilizing the pyrolysis off-gas to chemically reduce the metal oxide to elemental metal, such as iron. This application claims the benefit of U.S. Provisional Patent Application No. 63/083,223 filed Sep. 25, 2020, which is incorporated herein by reference in its entirety. All publications, patents, and patent applications mentioned in this specification are herein incorporated by reference to the same extent as if each individual publication, patent, or patent application was specifically and individually indicated to be incorporated by reference. The present disclosure relates to processes, systems, and apparatus for the processing of metal ores to produce metals using carbon-containing reagents. Biomass is a term used to describe biologically produced matter. The chemical energy contained in biomass is derived from solar energy using the natural process of photosynthesis. This is the process by which plants take in carbon dioxide and water from their surroundings and, using energy from sunlight, convert them into sugars, starches, cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Of all the renewable energy sources, biomass is unique in that it is, effectively, stored solar energy. Furthermore, biomass is the only renewable source of carbon. Carbonaceous materials for industrial use are commonly sourced from fossil resources, such as natural gas, petroleum, coal, and lignite, while renewable resources such as lignocellulosic biomass and various carbon-rich waste materials are of increasing interest. There exist a variety of conversion technologies to convert biomass feedstocks into carbonaceous materials. Increased use of biomass based carbonaceous materials poses technical and economic challenges arising from feedstock variations, operational difficulties, and capital intensity. There has been less focus on improving pyrolysis processes specifically for optimizing yield and quality of the solids as high-carbon reagents. Historically, slow pyrolysis of wood has been performed in large piles, in a simple batch process, with no emissions control. Traditional charcoal-making technologies are energy-inefficient as well as highly polluting. Clearly, there are economic and practical challenges to scaling up such a process for continuous commercial-scale production of high-quality carbon, while managing the energy balance and controlling emissions. Metal processing is an enormously important industry on a global basis. For example, with respect to steel (alloys of iron), the global steel market size is expected to reach $1 trillion USD by 2025, according to Steel Market Size, Share & Trends Analysis 2018-2025, Grand View Research, Inc. (2017). Growing inclination of contractors towards sustainable, low-cost, and durable building materials is driving steel demand in industrial infrastructure and residential projects. In pre-engineered metal buildings with high structural integrity, steel plays an essential function in stability, design flexibility, and aesthetic appeal. Stringent regulations promoting green and energy-efficient buildings are also contributing to steel demand, especially in industrial structures. About 70% of all steel is made from pig iron produced by reducing iron oxide in a blast furnace using coke or coal before reduction in an oxygen-blown converter. The use of non-renewable coal or coal-derived coke causes non-renewable carbon dioxide to be emitted into the atmosphere, in addition to depleting fossil resources. Oxygenated iron ores are mined globally. Typically, iron ores are taken through a beneficiation process to grind and concentrate the iron fraction, then rolled into pellets (with binders) and heated in an induration furnace, burning coal for heat, to harden the pellets for shipment to a blast furnace where coke is used to reduce the oxygenated ore to metallic iron. The induration and coking processes create massive amounts of CO 2 and other pollutants. Generally speaking, metals processing causes significant global net CO 2 emissions annually. For example, one of the biggest drawbacks of conventional blast furnaces is the inevitable carbon dioxide production as iron is reduced from iron oxides by carbon. Steelmaking is one of the largest industrial contributors of CO 2 emissions in the world today. There is a strong desire to make metal-making processes more environmentally friendly. In view of the aforementioned needs, there is a commercial desire for improved processes and systems for converting metal ores to metals. Carbon-based reagents can be produced, in theory, from virtually any material containing carbon. It is preferable to utilize renewable biomass to produce carbon-based reagents because of the rising economic, environmental, and social costs associated with fossil resources. Pyrolysis is a process for thermal conversion of solid materials in the complete absence of oxidizing agent (air or oxygen), or with such limited supply that oxidation does not occur to any appreciable extent. Depending on process conditions and additives, biomass pyrolysis can be adjusted to produce widely varying amounts of gas, liquid, and solid. Lower process temperatures and longer vapor residence times favor the production of solids. High temperatures and longer residence times increase the biomass conversion to syngas, while moderate temperatures and short vapor residence times are generally optimum for producing liquids. There is a need for technological advances in pyrolysis and related processes for converting biomass into high-quality syngas or to liquids as precursors to liquid fuels. The present disclosure addresses the deficiencies in the field and relates to processes, systems, and apparatus for the processing of metal ores to produce metals using carbon-containing reagents. Disclosed herein are processes for reducing a metal ore. title: Methods and apparatus for enhancing the energy content of carbonaceous materials from pyrolysis
text: Methods and apparatus for enhancing the energy content of carbonaceous materials from pyrolysis Processes and systems for converting biomass into high-carbon biogenic reagents that are suitable for a variety of commercial applications. Pyrolysis in the presence of an inert gas is employed to generate hot pyrolyzed solids, condensable vapors, and non-condensable gases, followed by separation of vapors and gases, and cooling of the hot pyrolyzed solids in the presence of the inert gas. Additives may be introduced during processing or combined with the reagent, or both. The biogenic reagent may include at least 70 wt %, 80 wt %, 90 wt %, 95 wt %, or more total carbon on a dry basis. The biogenic reagent may have an energy content of at least 12,000 Btu/lb, 13,000 Btu/lb, 14,000 Btu/lb, or 14,500 Btu/lb on a dry basis. The biogenic reagent may be formed into fine powders, or structural objects. The structural objects may have a structure and/or strength that derive from the feedstock, heat rate, and additives. The present invention generally relates to processes, systems, and apparatus for the production of high-carbon biogenic reagents, and compositions, products, and uses related thereto. Carbon is a platform element in a wide variety of industries and has a vast number of chemical, material, and fuel uses. Carbon is a good fuel to produce energy, including electricity. Carbon also has tremendous chemical value for various commodities and advanced materials, including metals, metal alloys, composites, carbon fibers, electrodes, and catalyst supports. For metal making, carbon is useful as a reactant, for reducing metal oxides to metals during processing; as a fuel, to provide heat for processing; and as a component of the final metal alloy. Carbon is a very important element in steel since it allows steel to be hardened by heat treatment. Carbon-based reagents can be produced, in principle, from virtually any material containing carbon. Carbonaceous materials commonly include fossil resources such as natural gas, petroleum, coal, and lignite; and renewable resources such as lignocellulosic biomass and various carbon-rich waste materials. Biomass is a term used to describe any biologically produced matter, or biogenic matter. The chemical energy contained in biomass is derived from solar energy using the natural process of photosynthesis. This is the process by which plants take in carbon dioxide and water from their surroundings and, using energy from sunlight, convert them into sugars, starches, cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Of all the renewable energy sources, biomass is unique in that it is, effectively, stored solar energy. Furthermore, biomass is the only renewable source of carbon. By utilizing biogenic carbon for fuel, CO 2 emissions associated with the combustion do not contribute to net life-cycle carbon emissions because carbon is recycled to grow more biomass. Also, use of biogenic carbon as a fuel will typically cause lower emissions of sulfur dioxide and mercury, compared to use of coal or other solid fossil fuels for energy production. For chemical and material applications in which the carbon will not be immediately combusted, by utilizing biogenic carbon, the carbon can be effectively sequestered for long periods of time (e.g., when carbon is added to steel for permanent structures). In this way, the net carbon emissions are actually negativeâCO 2 from the atmosphere is used to grow biogenic feedstocks and then the carbon is sequestered in biogenic products. Converting biomass to high-carbon reagents, however, poses both technical as well as economic challenges arising from feedstock variations, operational difficulties, and capital intensity. There exist a variety of conversion technologies to turn biomass feedstocks into high-carbon materials. Most of the known conversion technologies utilize some form of pyrolysis. Pyrolysis is a process for thermal conversion of solid materials in the complete absence of oxidizing agent (air or oxygen), or with such limited supply that oxidation does not occur to any appreciable extent. Depending on process conditions and additives, biomass pyrolysis can be adjusted to produce widely varying amounts of gas, liquid, and solid. Lower process temperatures and longer vapor residence times favor the production of solids. High temperatures and longer residence times increase the biomass conversion to syngas, while moderate temperatures and short vapor residence times are generally optimum for producing liquids. Recently, there has been much attention devoted to pyrolysis and related processes for converting biomass into high-quality syngas and/or to liquids as precursors to liquid fuels. On the other hand, there has been less focus on improving pyrolysis processes specifically for optimizing yield and quality of the solids as high-carbon reagents. Historically, slow pyrolysis of wood has been performed in large piles, in a simple batch process, with no emissions control. Traditional charcoal-making technologies are energy-inefficient as well as highly polluting. Clearly, there are economic and practical challenges to scaling up such a process for continuous commercial-scale production of high-quality carbon, while managing the energy balance and controlling emissions.
