title: Hybrid biorefining and gasification of lignocellulosic feedstocks
text: Hybrid biorefining and gasification of lignocellulosic feedstocks Processes and systems for concurrent recovery of lignin derivatives and syngas from a lignocellulosic feedstock. The processes and systems therefor generally comprise the steps of: (a) perfusing and cooking the lignocellulosic feedstock with a suitable organic solvent for a suitable period of time thereby producing a cellulosic solids output stream and a spent liquid solvent stream, said spent liquid solvent stream comprising solubilized lignin derivatives and other organic compounds; (b) separating said cellulosic solids output stream and said spent liquid solvent stream; (c) recovering lignin derivatives from the spent liquid solvent stream thereby producing at least a partially de-lignified spent liquid solvent stream; (d) recovering a portion of the organic solvent from the at least partially de-lignified spent liquid solvent stream thereby producing a stillage; and (e) gasifying the cellulosic solids output stream thereby producing a combustible syngas. What is claimed is: 1. A process for concurrent recovery of lignin derivatives and syngas from a lignocellulosic feedstock, the process comprising the steps of: perfusing and cooking the lignocellulosic feedstock with an organic solvent for a suitable period of time thereby producing a cellulosic solids output stream and a spent liquid solvent stream, said spent liquid solvent stream comprising solubilized lignin derivatives and other organic compounds; separating said cellulosic solids output stream and said spent liquid solvent stream; recovering lignin derivatives from the spent liquid solvent stream thereby producing at least a partially de-lignified spent liquid solvent stream; recovering a portion of the organic solvent from the at least partially de- lignified spent liquid solvent stream thereby producing a stillage; and gasifying the cellulosic solids output stream thereby producing a combustible syngas. 2. A process according to claim 1, wherein the stillage is concurrently gasified with the cellulosic solids output stream. 3. A process according to claim 1, wherein the at least partially de-lignified solids output stream is further processed to remove therefrom at least one furfurals, acetic acid, sugar syrups, phenolic compounds and terpenoids, thereby producing a processed stillage waste stream. 4. A process according to claim 3, wherein the processed stillage waste stream is concurrently gasified with the cellulosic solids output stream. 5. A process according to claim 1, wherein the combustible syngas is further processed to recover therefrom a short-chain alcohol. 6. A process according to claim 5, wherein the short-chain alcohol is one of methanol, ethanol, and butanol. 7. A process according to claim 5, wherein further processing of the combustible syngas is one of a chemical reaction and a fermentation. -12- 8. A process according to claim 7, wherein said chemical reaction comprises at least one reaction step of contacting the syngas with a suitable catalyst. 9. A process according to claim 1, wherein the combustible syngas is further processed to recover therefrom at least one of alkanes, olefins, oxygenates and biodiesel. 10. A process according to claim 9, wherein the further processing comprises at least one Fischer-Tropsch reaction. 11. A biorefining system for recovering lignin derivatives from lignocellulosic feedstocks, the system comprising: a pulping unit configured to receive and process a lignocellulosic feedstock with an organic solvent to separate therefrom a cellulosic solids stream and a spent solvent black liquor stream comprising solubilized plant components; a black liquor processing unit configured to receive and process the black liquor stream for separation and recovery therefrom of a plurality of lignin derivatives, a portion of the organic solvent, and at least a partially de-lignified stillage; and a gasification unit configured to receive and gasify the cellulosic solids stream and to recover therefrom a syngas stream. 12. A biorefining system according to claim 11, additionally configured to recycle the recovered portion of the organic solvent into the pulping unit. 13. A biorefining system according to claim 11, wherein the black liquor processing unit is additionally configured for recovery from the de-lignified stillage of at least one of furfurals, acetic acid, sugar syrups, phenolic compounds and terpenoids, thereby producing a de-lignified stillage waste stream. 14. A biorefining system according to claim 11, additionally configured to recycle the recovered portion of the de-lignified stillage into the gasification unit. 15. A biorefining system according to claim 13, additionally configured to recycle the recovered portion of the de-lignified stillage waste stream into the gasification unit. -13- 16. A biorefining system according to claim 11, wherein the gasification unit is additionally configured to convert a portion of the syngas stream into a short- chain alcohol. 17. A biorefining system according to claim 16, wherein the gasification unit is configured for purification of the syngas stream. 18. A biorefining system according to claim 16, wherein the gasification unit is configured for conversion of the syngas stream into a short-chain alcohol by at least one catalyzed chemical reaction. 19. A biorefining system according to claim 16, wherein the gasification unit is configured for conversion of the syngas stream into a short-chain alcohol by a fermentation process. 20. A biorefining system according to claim 11, wherein the gasification unit is additionally configured to convert a portion of the syngas stream into one of alkanes, olefins, oxygenates and biodiesel by a Fischer-Tropsch reaction. 21. A biorefining system according to claim 11, wherein the gasification unit is configured for concurrent conversion of a portion of the syngas stream into a short-chain alcohol and one of alkanes, olefins, oxygenates and biodiesel. 22. A modular biorefining system for recovering lignin derivatives from lignocellulosic feedstocks, the system comprising: a first module comprising a pulping unit configured to receive and process a lignocellulosic feedstock with an organic solvent to separate therefrom a cellulosic solids stream and a black liquor stream comprising solubilized plant components; a second module comprising a black liquor processing unit configured to receive and process the black liquor stream to separate and recover therefrom a plurality of lignin derivatives, a portion of the organic solvent, and a de-lignified stillage; and a third module comprising a gasification unit configured to receive and gasify the cellulosic solids stream and to recover therefrom a syngas stream. -14- 23. A modular biorefining system according to claim 22, additionally provided with a fourth module configured for receiving and processing therein a portion of the cellulosic solids stream from the first module. -15-

title: Pyrolysis of lignin
text: Pyrolysis of lignin One aspect of the present invention relates to a method of modifying thermoplastic properties of lignin rich biomass to reduce agglomeration during any subsequent pyrolysis. The method comprises providing a lignin rich biomass and treating the lignin rich biomass with an alkali metal hydroxide or an alkaline earth metal hydroxide under conditions effective to reduce agglomeration, during any subsequent pyrolysis, compared to when the lignin rich biomass is not subjected to said treating. Also disclosed is a method of fast pyrolysis using the product of this method of modifying the thermoplastic properties of lignin rich biomass. One aspect of the present invention relates to a method of modifying thermoplastic properties of lignin rich biomass to reduce agglomeration during any subsequent pyrolysis. The method comprises providing a lignin rich biomass and treating the lignin rich biomass with an alkali metal hydroxide or an alkaline earth metal hydroxide under conditions effective to reduce agglomeration, during any subsequent pyrolysis, compared to when the lignin rich biomass is not subjected to said treating. Also disclosed is a method of fast pyrolysis using the product of this method of modifying the thermoplastic properties of lignin rich biomass. This application claims the benefit of U.S. Provisional Patent Application Ser. No. 62/297,605, filed Feb. 19, 2016, which is hereby incorporated by reference in its entirety. The present invention relates to the preparation of lignin for fast pyrolysis. Lignin is the second most abundant natural polymer in the biosphere followed by cellulose, accounting for up to 30% of lignocellulosic biomass. Over 50 million tons of so-called technical lignin is annually extracted from lignocellulosic biomass as a byproduct of the pulp and paper industry with increasing amounts from the emerging cellulosic ethanol industry (Ragauskas et al., âLignin Valorization: Improving Lignin Processing in the Biorefinery,â Science 344(6185):1246843 (2014) and Azadi et al., âLiquid Fuels, Hydrogen and Chemicals from Lignin: a Critical Review,â Renew. Sust. Energ. Rev. 21:506-523 (2013)). Lignin is a phenylpropane-based polymer biosynthesized from random polymerization of three precursor monomers. Because of its abundance and availability in low cost, lignin has potential as a renewable source of aromatics. At present, most lignin is burned as boiler fuel while only 2% of it is upgraded to biobased products, such as binder, resin, and dispersant (Huber et al., âSynthesis of Transportation Fuels from Biomass: Chemistry, Catalysts, and Engineering,â Chem. Rev. 106:4044-4098 (2006); Zakzeski et al., âThe Catalystic Valorization of Lignin for the Production of Renewable Chemicals,â Chem. Rev. 110:3552-99 (2010); Effendi et al., âProduction of Renewable Phenolic Resins by Thermochemical Conversion of Biomass: A Review,â Renew. Sust. Energ. Rev. 12:2092-2116 (2008); and Lange et al., âOxidative Upgrade of LigninâRecent Routes Reviewed,â Eur. Polym. J. 49:1151-1173 (2013)). Developing effective upgrading methods to convert lignin into value-added products could reduce dependency on petroleum and also improve the economic prospects for companies producing lignin as a co-product of biomass processing. Depolymerizing lignin by either biological or thermochemical means has been extensively studied over the past several decades (Perez et al., âBiodegradation and Biological Treatments of Cellulose, Hemicellulose and Lignin: An Overview,â Int. Microbiol. 5:53-63 (2002); Salvachua et al., âTowards Lignin Consolidated Bioprocessing: Simultaneous Lignin Depolymerization and Product Generation by Bacteria,â Green Chem. 17:4951-4967 (2015); Pandey et al., âLignin Depolymerization and Conversion: a Review of Thermochemical Methods,â Chem. Eng. Technol. 34:29-41 (2011); and Amen-Chen et al., âProduction of Monomeric Phenols by Thermochemical Conversion of Biomass: A Review,â Bioresource Technol. 79:277-299 (2001)). Solvent liquefaction using a variety of solvents at elevated temperatures and pressures is the most common method for deconstructing lignin (Jin et al., âLiquefaction of Lignin by Polyethyleneglycol and Glycerol,â Bioresource Technol. 102:3581-3583 (2011); Kang et al., âHydrothermal Conversion of Lignin: A Review,â Renew. Sust. Energ. Rev. 27:546-558 (2013) and Kleinert et al., âOptimizing Solvolysis Conditions for Integrated Depolymerisation and Hydrodeoxygenation of Lignin to Produce Liquid Biofuel,â J. Anal., Appl. Pyrol. 85:108-117 (2009)). Despite the advantages of solvent liquefaction, the consumption of solvent and the need for separating reaction products from solvent, char and/or catalysts present both economic and technical challenges. Fast pyrolysis is an alternative thermal depolymerization technique. Fast pyrolysis has been widely explored for the conversion of whole plant biomass into liquid products (Bridgwater et al., âAn Overview of Fast Pyrolysis of Biomass,â Org. Geochem. 30:1479-1493 (1999); Mohan et al., âPyrolysis of Wood/Biomass for Bio-Oil: A Critical Review,â Energ. Fuel 20:848-889 (2006) and Bridgwater âUpgrading Biomass Fast Pyrolysis Liquids,â Environ. Prog. Sust. Energ. 31:261-268 (2012)). Fast pyrolysis rapidly heats the feedstock (usually <2 s) in the absence of oxygen and usually at atmospheric pressure. Lignocellulosic biomass is substantially decomposed to form liquid, called bio-oil, char, and non-condensable gases. Bio-oil from fast pyrolysis is similar to the liquid produced by solvent liquefaction. It can be upgraded to hydrocarbon fuels or other chemicals. The char product (also known as biochar) has several applications such as solid fuel, soil amendment and activated carbon (Laird et al., âReview of the Pyrolysis Platform for Coproducing Bio-Oil and Biochar,â Biofuel Bioprod Bior. 3:547-562 (2009)). Despite its potential, fast pyrolysis of technical lignin has been infrequently studied, usually limited to batch experiments involving only small quantities of lignin (Ben et al., âPyrolysis of Kraft Ligning with Additives,â Energ. Fuel 25:4662-4668 (2011); Kosa et al., âPyrolysis Oils from CO 2 Precipitated Kraft Lignin,â Green Chem. 13:3196-3202 (2011) and Sharma et al., âCharacterization of Chars From Pyrolysis of Lignin,â Fuel 83:1469-1482 (2004)). Although these previous studies have provided valuable insight into lignin depolymerization, continuous pyrolysis relevant to commercial applications are lacking (De Wild et al., âLignin Pyrolysis for Profitable Lignocellulosic Biorefineries,â Biofuel Bioprod. Bior. 8:645-657 (2014)). Efforts to continuously pyrolyze lignin have been largely unsuccessful due to the melting and subsequent agglomeration of lignin particles to form âhard shellâ solid material, which clogs the reactor and forces shut-down. This problem was highlighted by an international collaboration in 2010 (Nowakowski et al., âLignin Fast Pyrolysis: Results From an International Collaboration,â J. Anal., Appl. Pyrol. 88:53-72 (2010)). Two types of lignin, one from soda pulping of non-woody biomass and the other from weak acid hydrolysis of softwood, were distributed to seven laboratories for pyrolysis in small-scale, fluidized bed pyrolyzer. None of the laboratories were able to pyrolyze the soda pulp lignin due to plugging of the feeder or defluidization of the reactor. Pyrolysis of the acid hydrolysis lignin was only marginally better, possibly because of the presence of a large amount of carbohydrate in this particular feedstock. Several researchers have attempted to pyrolyze lignin by adding cooling jackets or making other design changes to the feeder tubes, installing mechanical stirrers inside the reactors, pelletizing lignin, or performing pyrolysis in the presence of oxygen (Li et al., âOxidative Pyrolysis of Kraft Lignin in a Bubbling Fluidized Bed Reactor With Air,â Biomass Bioenerg. 76:96-107 (2015); Trinh et al., âFast Pyrolysis of Lignin Using a Pyrolysis Centrifuge Reactor,â Energ. Fuel 27:3802-3810 (2013); and Tumbalam Gooty et al., âKraft-Lignin Pyrolysis and Fractional Condensation of its Bio-Oil Vapors,â J. Anal., Pyrol. 106:33-40 (2014)). None of these efforts were completely successful in eliminating agglomeration. In a recent review paper, Ragauskas et al., âLignin Valorization: Improving Lignin Processing in the Biorefinery,â Science 344(6185):1246843 (2014) warned that the inability to continuously feed lignin to large-scale reactors is the primary technical barrier to pyrolyzing lignin for the production of fuels and chemicals. Pretreating lignin is another approach to improving the pyrolysis of lignin. Mukkamala et al., âFormate-assisted Fast Pyrolysis of Lignin,â Energ. Fuel 26:1380-1384 (2012) pretreated an acid hydrolyzed kraft lignin with 50-100% weight equivalence of calcium formate using a two-step process before pyrolysis in an entrained flow reactor. In their study, fluidizing sand was removed from the reactor during pyrolysis in order to avoid agglomeration between sand and lignin particles. WO 2011159154 A1 to Wilberink et al. describes a slurry of lignin and clay (1:1 weight ratio) mixed in water and extruded as pellets and then dried in a two-step heat treatment prior to pyrolysis. Upon pyrolysis in an auger reactor, phenolic-rich bio-oil was produced. The solid residue from pyrolysis of lignin-clay pellets were pellets containing char and the clay binder. See Wilberink et al. De Wild et al., âLignin Pyrolysis for Profitable Lignocellulosic Biorefineries,â Biofuel Bioprod. Bior. 8:645-657 (2014) also pyrolyzed in a fluidized bed the pellets formed from the lignin co-product of organosolv processing of straw. They concluded that a dedicated feeding system and careful control of pyrolysis conditions are required to pyrolyze lignin even when pelletized. Because of this difficulty of pyrolyzing lignin, the products of lignin pyrolysis have yet to be fully characterized. One previous study reported the composition of pyrolysis vapor but not char (De Wild et al., âLignin Pyrolysis for Profitable Lignocellulosic Biorefineries,â Biofuel Bioprod. Bior. 8:645-657 (2014)). A study conducted by Sharma et al., âCharacterization of Chars From Pyrolysis of Lignin,â Fuel 83:1469-1482 (2004) characterized the agglomerated char produced from slow pyrolysis of lignin in a batch reactor but did not give information about volatile products. The present invention is directed to overcoming the deficiencies in the art by treating lignin to prevent its melting and subsequence agglomeration upon heating, and preventing difficulties that can arise from lignin agglomeration during pyrolysis, and allowing for continuous pyrolysis in a fluidized reactor. One aspect of the present invention relates to a method of modifying thermoplastic properties of lignin rich biomass to reduce agglomeration during any subsequent pyrolysis. The method comprises providing a lignin rich biomass and treating the lignin rich biomass with an alkali metal hydroxide or an alkaline earth metal hydroxide under conditions effective to reduce agglomeration, during any subsequent pyrolysis, compared to when the lignin rich biomass is not subjected to said treating. Another aspect of the present invention relates to a method of fast pyrolysis. The method comprises providing a lignin rich biomass, treating the lignin rich biomass with an alkali metal hydroxide or an alkaline earth metal hydroxide under conditions effective to reduce agglomeration, during pyrolysis, compared to when the lignin rich biomass is not subjected to said treating, and pyrolyzing the treated lignin rich biomass to produce pyrolysis products. Applicants believe that lignin would have to be chemically modified to prevent its melting and subsequent agglomeration upon heating. The present invention is a simple chemical pretreatment of lignin that prevents its agglomeration. The properties of the resulting pyrolysis products are described, and applicants propose a mechanism by which pretreatment prevents lignin agglomeration. The benefits of the present invention include the ability to fast pyrolyze lignin without modifying existing equipment. The alkali metal hydroxide or alkaline earth metal hydroxides are present in low ratios to lignin rich biomass, have low material cost, high availability, are easy to recover by burning char and leaching the ash with water, and some have low risk hazard. The heat of combustion from this regeneration process can be used to heat the pyrolyzer. Reduced agglomeration of lignin during fast pyrolysis creates the opportunity for producing liquid products rich in phenolic monomers and dimers, which could be used as chemicals or upgraded for hydrocarbon fuels, and bio-char, which could be used as fertilizer. This would be achieved with reduced handling time and operating costs compared to solvent liquefaction methods for processing lignin. In addition, the pretreatment process could be integrated into the lignin extraction process, further reducing operating costs.
